Zhujiajiao was peaceful and beautiful, with charming canals, bridges, and old streets that felt very different from central Shanghai. Yu Garden and the surrounding area were lively and full of traditional architecture, local shops, and food options. Transport and timing were organized smoothly, and everything felt quite stress-free despite covering multiple locations. The guide managed the group well and gave useful explanations and tips throughout the tour. A great option if you want to see both old and modern Shanghai without planning all the logistics yourself. content: I've brought relatives and friends to Yu Garden many times, but each time we only visited the Nine-Turn Bridge, the Green Wave Corridor, and the Lake Pavilion. Today, I discovered that the garden itself is a hidden gem. Every stone, every hill, every tree, every lion, dragon, toad, and mud brick sculpture, all unfolded before me through the flowing river of history, thanks to Teacher Mao's eloquent narration. The Jade Linglong Stone, a relic of Emperor Huizong of Song's "Flower and Stone Tribute," the iron lion still gleaming from the Yuan Dynasty, the imposing and beautiful rockery, the 400-year-old ginkgo tree, and the Dianchun Hall, which witnessed the rise and fall of the Pan Mansion, the Sugar Industry Guild, and the Small Swords Society—all speak of aesthetics and the passage of time. Thank you, Teacher Mao, for your wonderful and vivid explanation. Leaving the garden, I revisited the Nine-Turn Bridge and the Green Wave Corridor, savoring the pavilions, terraces, flowers, rocks, and plants behind them, and bought a butterfly pastry, the same kind used by British Prime Minister Starmer. I'm already thinking that next time friends visit, I'll definitely bring them to appreciate the cultural atmosphere of this place again.
